# Spectral numerical methods {#sec-spectral-methods}

A spectral method approximates a field by a finite sum of global basis functions.
It solves for their coefficients rather than for independent values in each cell.
The basis should respect the domain: Fourier modes suit periodic intervals,
orthogonal polynomials suit bounded intervals, and spherical harmonics suit the
sphere. The [function-space chapter](../02-harmonic-analysis/function-spaces.qmd)
explains projection; here we turn projection into a numerical method.

## From a PDE to coefficient equations

Let $u(x,t)$ be a scalar field on a domain $D$, and let $\{\varphi_j\}$ be an
orthonormal basis for a specified inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$.
For $J$ retained functions, write

$$
u_J(x,t)=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}a_j(t)\varphi_j(x).
$$

For a PDE $\partial_t u=\mathcal{L}u+\mathcal{N}(u)+g$, a Galerkin method
requires the residual to be orthogonal to every retained basis function:

$$
\frac{da_i}{dt}
=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\langle\mathcal{L}\varphi_j,\varphi_i\rangle a_j
 +\langle\mathcal{N}(u_J),\varphi_i\rangle
 +\langle g,\varphi_i\rangle.
$$

Here $\mathcal{L}$ is linear, $\mathcal{N}$ contains nonlinear terms, and $g$ is
forcing. A nonorthonormal basis introduces a mass matrix
$M_{ij}=\langle\varphi_j,\varphi_i\rangle$ on the left.
Boundary conditions must be built into the basis or imposed separately.
A **collocation method** instead sets the residual to zero at selected nodes.
A **pseudospectral method** evaluates terms through transformations between
coefficients and node values. With adequate quadrature and dealiasing, its
computed nonlinear projection can agree with Galerkin projection.
These distinctions concern spatial discretization; time integration is a
separate numerical choice. See @Boyd2001spectral for the general framework.

For a periodic interval $[0,2\pi)$, $\partial_x e^{ikx}=ik e^{ikx}$ and
$\partial_x^2e^{ikx}=-k^2e^{ikx}$. Differentiation becomes coefficient
multiplication. With physical coordinate $s=Rx$, the derivative is instead
$\partial_s=R^{-1}\partial_x$, so its units are inverse length.

## Why global expansions can be accurate

For an orthonormal basis, the squared $L^2$ truncation error is the energy in
omitted coefficients. Rapid coefficient decay therefore gives rapid convergence.
For periodic analytic functions that extend analytically into a complex strip,
Fourier coefficients decay exponentially with mode number. Finite regularity
usually gives algebraic decay. Discontinuities cause oscillations near jumps
and slow convergence; increasing the truncation alone does not remove the
Gibbs phenomenon. Spectral accuracy depends on regularity and compatible
boundary conditions, not merely on choosing a transform.

A global method is useful when smooth solutions need high accuracy, derivatives
or elliptic inversions have simple coefficient formulas, or scale-dependent
analysis is central. Local methods may be preferable for shocks, complex
boundaries, local refinement, or localized communication.

## Spherical harmonic representation

Use colatitude $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, longitude $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$, latitude
$\alpha=\pi/2-\theta$, and radius $R>0$ in metres. Define
$\mu=\cos\theta=\sin\alpha$. Solid angle is dimensionless:

$$
d\Omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=d\mu\,d\phi
$$

when the $\mu$ integral runs from $-1$ to $1$. Physical area is $R^2d\Omega$.
Use the orthonormal complex harmonics from the
[spherical harmonics chapter](../02-harmonic-analysis/spherical-harmonics.qmd).
For $m\ge0$, their associated Legendre functions include the Condon--Shortley
phase:

$$
P_\ell^m(\mu)=(-1)^m(1-\mu^2)^{m/2}
\frac{d^mP_\ell}{d\mu^m},
\qquad
Y_\ell^m=N_{\ell m}P_\ell^m(\mu)e^{im\phi},
\quad
N_{\ell m}=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}\frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}}.
$$

Negative orders satisfy $Y_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{Y_\ell^m}$.
Triangular truncation at degree $L$ retains

$$
f_L=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}
\widehat f_\ell^mY_\ell^m,
\qquad
\widehat f_\ell^m=\int_{S^2}f\overline{Y_\ell^m}\,d\Omega.
$$

There are $(L+1)^2$ complex basis functions. A real field obeys
$\widehat f_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{\widehat f_\ell^m}$, reducing independent
storage. If $f$ has units $U$, so do its coefficients under this dimensionless
normalization. Truncation degree and the number of stored modes differ by one
when degree zero is included.

## Gaussian grid and quadrature {#sec-gaussian-quadrature}

A quadrature rule approximates an integral by weighted function values.
The $n$-point Gauss--Legendre rule on $[-1,1]$ uses the roots $\mu_i$ of the
Legendre polynomial $P_n$ and positive weights

$$
\int_{-1}^{1}q(\mu)\,d\mu
\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iq(\mu_i),
\qquad
w_i=\frac{2}{(1-\mu_i^2)[P_n'(\mu_i)]^2}.
$$

It is exact for polynomials of degree at most $2n-1$, and
$\sum_iw_i=2$. @GolubWelsch1969 gives algorithms for computing Gaussian rules
from orthogonal-polynomial recurrences. The following argument explains why the
Legendre nodes give this exactness.

For a polynomial $q$ of degree at most $2n-1$, polynomial division gives
$q=P_ns+r$, where $s$ and $r$ have degree at most $n-1$. Legendre orthogonality
makes $\int P_ns=0$. At every node $P_n(\mu_i)=0$, so $q(\mu_i)=r(\mu_i)$.
Choose weights that integrate the Lagrange interpolant of $r$ exactly. The same
weighted sum then integrates $q$ exactly. The extra exact degrees come from
orthogonality, not from uniformly spacing the nodes.

A **full Gaussian grid** combines these nodes with $M$ equally spaced longitudes:

$$
\alpha_i=\arcsin\mu_i,\qquad
\phi_j=\frac{2\pi j}{M},\quad j=0,\ldots,M-1.
$$

Latitudes are not equally spaced, and no node is at a pole. An equatorial node
exists when $n$ is odd. Every latitude ring has the same $M$ longitudes; a reduced
Gaussian grid instead varies their count and needs a corresponding transform
algorithm. The full-grid formulas below do not apply unchanged to a reduced grid.

The area integral and global mean are approximated by

$$
\int_{S_R^2}f\,dA
\approx R^2\frac{2\pi}{M}\sum_{i,j}w_if_{ij},
\qquad
\langle f\rangle_A\approx\frac{1}{2M}\sum_{i,j}w_if_{ij}.
$$

Thus a constant integrates to $4\pi R^2$. For a zonal profile, normalized latitude
weights are $w_i/2$. Do not multiply Gaussian weights by $\cos\alpha_i$ again:
the substitution $d\mu=\cos\alpha\,d\alpha$ already accounts for the area
Jacobian. Uniform weights per latitude ring would also be incorrect.

### Worked quadrature example

For $n=2$, the nodes are $\mu=\pm1/\sqrt3$ and both weights are one.
For $f=\mu^2$ the approximate global mean is

$$
\frac12\left[\left(-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2+
\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2\right]=\frac13,
$$

which equals $\frac12\int_{-1}^{1}\mu^2\,d\mu$.
The same rule gives $1/9$ for the mean of $\mu^4$, whereas its exact mean is
$1/5$. Degree four exceeds this rule's degree-three guarantee.

## Why this grid helps the SHT

The spherical harmonic transform (SHT) separates into longitude Fourier analysis
and latitude Legendre analysis. For $m\ge0$, define

$$
F_m(\mu_i)=\frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}f(\mu_i,\phi_j)e^{-im\phi_j}.
$$

Then compute

$$
\widehat f_\ell^m\approx
2\pi N_{\ell m}\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iF_m(\mu_i)P_\ell^m(\mu_i).
$$

An FFT computes all longitude coefficients on each ring. Associated Legendre
sums complete the forward transform; synthesis evaluates the harmonic sum at
nodes. See @Schaeffer2013sht for a practical transform algorithm.

For a field bandlimited to degree $L$, sufficient sampling conditions for exact
coefficient recovery in exact arithmetic are

$$
n\ge L+1,\qquad M\ge 2L+1.
$$

To see why, expand the input in retained harmonics. The longitude sum contains
$e^{i(m'-m)\phi_j}$ and is zero unless $m'=m$ under this sampling condition.
For the surviving terms,

$$
P_\ell^m(\mu)P_{\ell'}^m(\mu)
=(1-\mu^2)^m\frac{d^mP_\ell}{d\mu^m}
\frac{d^mP_{\ell'}}{d\mu^m},
$$

which is a polynomial of degree at most $\ell+\ell'\le2L$. Since
$2n-1\ge2L$, Gaussian quadrature integrates these products exactly. The discrete
inner product therefore reproduces orthogonality on the retained harmonic space.
This is why the nodes and weights are part of the transform definition.

The statement does not claim that each $P_\ell^m$ is itself a polynomial:
odd $m$ introduces a square root. The same-order product is polynomial.
Nor does it promise exact coefficients for arbitrary sampled fields with energy
above $L$. Such unresolved structure can alias into retained modes.

For the bandlimited field, discrete Parseval also follows:

$$
\frac{2\pi}{M}\sum_{i,j}w_i|f_L(\mu_i,\phi_j)|^2
=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}|\widehat f_\ell^m|^2.
$$

Round trips and this identity test normalization, weights, and coordinate order.
Reversing latitude requires reversing the data and weights together. A shifted
longitude origin requires consistent Fourier phases. Shape agreement alone does
not establish transform compatibility.

A direct separated implementation uses approximately
$O(nM\log M)$ work for longitude FFTs and $O(nL^2)$ for the Legendre stage.
For $n,M=O(L)$ the latter is cubic. An SHT is not simply a two-dimensional FFT.
Recurrences, symmetry, precomputation, and specialized algorithms change practical
costs and memory needs.

## Solving equations in spectral space

On a radius-$R$ sphere, the physical Laplace--Beltrami operator satisfies

$$
\Delta_{S_R^2}Y_\ell^m=-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{R^2}Y_\ell^m.
$$

For Poisson's equation $\Delta_{S_R^2}u=f$, the sphere has no boundary and a
constant is in the nullspace. A solution exists only when
$\int f\,d\Omega=0$. Fix the undetermined mean by setting
$\widehat u_0^0=0$. For every $\ell\ge1$,

$$
\widehat u_\ell^m=-\frac{R^2}{\ell(\ell+1)}\widehat f_\ell^m.
$$

For example, if $f=A Y_2^0$, then $u=-AR^2Y_2^0/6$.
Applying the Laplacian recovers $f$, checking the sign and radius factor.
If $f$ has units $U\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$, $u$ has units $U$.

For diffusion $\partial_t u=\kappa\Delta_{S_R^2}u$, with diffusivity
$\kappa$ in $\mathrm{m}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1}$,

$$
\widehat u_\ell^m(t)=\widehat u_\ell^m(0)
\exp\left[-\frac{\kappa\ell(\ell+1)}{R^2}t\right].
$$

The mean remains constant and smaller scales decay faster. If forward Euler is
used instead of this exact update, stability for all retained diffusion modes
requires $\Delta t\le2R^2/[\kappa L(L+1)]$ for $L\ge1$.
Accurate spatial differentiation does not remove time-step restrictions.

## Nonlinear terms and aliasing

A product of fields bandlimited to $L$ can contain degrees up to $2L$.
Computing it on the minimally sampled grid and transforming back can fold
unresolved modes into lower degrees. In a periodic example, grid samples cannot
distinguish Fourier modes $k$ and $k+M$ because
$e^{i(k+M)2\pi j/M}=e^{ik2\pi j/M}$.

For exact projection of a product of two scalar degree-$L$ fields onto degrees
through $L$, a sufficient full Gaussian grid satisfies

$$
M>3L,\qquad 2n-1\ge3L.
$$

The longitude integrand contains three mode factors. Its maximum frequency is
$3L$. Surviving latitude products also have degree at most $3L$: the longitude
selection rule makes the sum of their absolute orders even, so the factors of
$(1-\mu^2)^{1/2}$ combine into an integer power. Gaussian exactness then applies.
This is the spherical counterpart of padding each dimension by roughly $3/2$
for a quadratic product. Strict inequalities and integer rounding matter.
Derivatives of vector components and higher-order nonlinearities require their
own analysis; these bounds apply to scalar products as stated.

A pseudospectral step therefore synthesizes on an adequate grid, evaluates the
nonlinear expression there, analyzes it, and retains only the intended modes.
Filtering damps selected coefficients but does not retroactively make an aliased
projection exact. Dealiasing, physical diffusion, and numerical filtering serve
different purposes.

## Uses and numerical checks

Spectral coefficients support elliptic inversion, diffusion, scale-dependent
filtering, energy spectra, and comparison across resolutions. A scalar isotropic
linear filter multiplies all orders at degree $\ell$ by the same factor; this
preserves rotational symmetry. General position-dependent coefficients couple
modes and need not yield diagonal operators.

Before using a transform in a solver, verify a constant, an individual harmonic,
a forward/inverse round trip, and discrete Parseval. Check an analytic PDE
solution such as the diffusion mode above. Increase truncation and quadrature
resolution separately: convergence in one does not demonstrate convergence in
the other. Record basis normalization, phase convention, radius, retained degrees,
node coordinates, and weights so that stored coefficients remain interpretable.
